name: Departmental Test Paper III: Account Code and Budget Manual

lessons.title: Classification Of Accounts (1)
lessons.source: KAC Vol I, Art. 24(a) Main division of accounts; KAC Vol I, Art. 24(b); KAC Vol I, Art. 26(a) Major, minor and detailed heads; KAC Vol I, Art. 26(c); KAC Vol I, Art. 27; KAC Vol I, Art. 28 Charged or Voted; KAC Vol I, Art. 29 Classification: limitations; KAC Vol I, Art. 30 General principle of class
points: The Comptroller and Auditor General, with the approval of the President, decides the classification of any transaction or class of transactions.
Classification refers mainly to the function, programme and activity of Government and the object of the revenue or expenditure, rather than the department.
Government accounts are kept in three parts: Part I, Part II and Part III.
Part I has two main divisions: Revenue, and Capital, Public Debt, Loans, etc.
The major head is the main unit of classification. Major, minor, sub-head and detailed head with sectors make a five tier structure.
The detailed head is the fifth and last tier of classification. It is the object classification.
Introducing a new major or minor head, or abolishing or renaming existing heads, needs approval of the Comptroller and Auditor General.
Voted expenditure is shown separately from charged expenditure. The words Charged or Voted are appended to the heads concerned.
remember: The Comptroller and Auditor General, with the President's approval, decides classification of any transaction.
Government accounts are kept in three parts. Part I has Revenue, and Capital, Public Debt, Loans etc.
Major head is the main unit; detailed head is the fifth and last tier (object classification).

questions.q: Who decides the classification of any transaction in Government accounts?
options: The Finance Secretary, with the approval of the Governor
The Accountant General, with the approval of the Governor
The Comptroller and Auditor General, with the approval of the President
The Comptroller and Auditor General, with the approval of the Finance Minister
questions.why: KAC Vol I, Art. 29: the CAG with the President's approval is the authority.

questions.q: Classification of transactions has closer reference to which of these?
options: The department that spends the money
Function, programme and activity, and the object of revenue or expenditure
The treasury that pays the bill
The Government servant who draws the money
questions.why: KAC Vol I, Art. 30: closer reference to function, programme, activity and object, rather than the department.

questions.q: Into how many parts are Government accounts kept?
questions.why: KAC Vol I, Art. 24(a): accounts are kept in three parts.

questions.q: What is the main unit of classification in accounts?
questions.why: KAC Vol I, Art. 26(a): the major head is the main unit of classification.

questions.q: Which tier of classification is the detailed head?
options: The third tier, the programme classification
The fourth tier, below the sub-head
The fifth and last tier, the object classification
The first tier, the function classification
questions.why: KAC Vol I, Art. 26(c): the detailed head is the fifth and last tier.

lessons.title: Classification Of Accounts (2)
lessons.source: KAC Vol I, Art. 33 Classification of PWD expenditure, item 4; KAC Vol I, Art. 33, item 3; KAC Vol I, Art. 33, item 5; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11 Definitions: Minor head; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11 Definitions: Sub-head; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 9(3); Kerala Budget Manual, Para 9(3) Five-tier
points: Major heads in the Revenue Receipts Section are assigned numbers 020 to 199.
Major heads in Capital Expenditure carry numbers 411 to 599. Revenue Expenditure heads carry 211 to 399.
The only major head in Part II, Contingency Fund, bears the number 800. Public Account heads are 801 to 899.
The minor head is the third tier of classification and denotes Plan or Non-Plan programmes undertaken by Government for a function.
The sub-head is the fourth tier of classification, immediately below the minor head.
Spending on Government residential buildings is accounted under major head 2216 Housing, or 4216 Capital Outlay on Housing.
Expenditure on roads and bridges is accounted under major head 3054 Roads and Bridges, or 5054 Capital Outlay on Roads and Bridges.
Maintenance and repairs of all Government non-residential buildings are accounted under major head 2059 Public Works.
remember: Major head blocks: Revenue Receipts 020-199, Revenue Expenditure 211-399, Capital Expenditure 411-599.
Contingency Fund is 800; Public Account heads are 801 to 899.
Residential buildings: 2216 / 4216. Roads and bridges: 3054 / 5054. Non-residential building repairs: 2059.

questions.q: What number block do major heads in the Revenue Receipts Section carry?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 9(3): Revenue Receipts are 020 to 199.

questions.q: Major heads in Capital Expenditure carry which numbers?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 9(3): Capital Expenditure is 411 to 599.

questions.q: Which major head number belongs to the Contingency Fund?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 9(3): the only major head in Part II, Contingency Fund, is 800.

questions.q: The minor head is which tier of classification?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11: the minor head is the third tier and denotes Plan or Non-Plan programmes.

questions.q: Under which major head is repair of Government non-residential buildings accounted?
questions.why: KAC Vol I, Art. 33, item 3: maintenance and repairs of non-residential buildings go to 2059 Public Works.

lessons.title: Grants (3)
lessons.source: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11 Definitions: Grant; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 4 Passing of the budget; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 87 Supplementary grant: definition; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 88(i) When required; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 89(1); Kerala Budget Manual, Para 89(1) Submission of propos
points: A grant is the sum sanctioned by the Legislature for a service or function, on a demand presented to it.
The Appropriation Act is the legal authority for withdrawing money from the Consolidated Fund and fixes the maximum for each service in the year.
A supplementary grant is a sum sanctioned by the Legislature for a service over and above the amount already authorised.
It is needed when the Appropriation Act amount is insufficient for a service, or when expenditure on a new service arises.
The expenditure could not be foreseen when original estimates were framed, and cannot in public interest be postponed to next year.
The Chief Controlling Officer has the primary responsibility for proposals for supplementary appropriations.
The Administrative Department examines the proposals and passes them to the Finance Department with its recommendations.
Article 205 of the Constitution requires a supplementary statement of estimated expenditure to be laid before the Legislature for a new service.
remember: A grant is the sum sanctioned by the Legislature for a service on a demand presented to it.
The Appropriation Act is the legal authority to withdraw from the Consolidated Fund.
Supplementary grant: over and above the amount already authorised. Chief Controlling Officer has primary responsibility.

questions.q: What is the legal authority for withdrawing money from the Consolidated Fund?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 4: the Appropriation Act is the legal authority and fixes the maximum for each service.

questions.q: What is a supplementary grant?
options: A sum sanctioned by the Finance Department from savings
A grant made to regularise past excess expenditure
The transfer of funds from one unit of appropriation to another
A sum sanctioned by the Legislature for a service over and above the amount already authorised
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 87: supplementary grant is over and above the amount already authorised.

questions.q: Who has primary responsibility for supplementary appropriation proposals?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 89(1): the Chief Controlling Officer has primary responsibility.

questions.q: The Administrative Department examines supplementary proposals and passes them to whom, with its recommendations?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 89(2): proposals go to the Finance Department with recommendations.

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution requires a supplementary statement for a new service?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 94(2): Article 205 requires a supplementary statement laid before the Legislature.

lessons.title: Grants (4)
lessons.source: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 94(2); Kerala Budget Manual, Para 95(3); Kerala Budget Manual, Para 96 Contingency Fund
points: No. No expenditure should be incurred on a new service, even if savings exist within the grant, before a supplementary grant is obtained.
If met from savings in the grant, a token sum of Rs. 100, or the balance actually required, is shown in the supplementary statement.
Interim provision is found by an advance from the Contingency Fund, pending authorisation by the Legislature.
The Contingency Fund was created under Article 267 (2) of the Constitution. It is like an imprest at the Governor's disposal.
The authority applies to the Administrative Department. With Finance concurrence, it may allow spending, with provision later by reappropriation or supplementary grant.
remember: No spending on a new service before a supplementary grant, even if savings exist.
Token sum Rs. 100 (or balance needed) is shown if met from savings.
Contingency Fund: Article 267 (2); advance given pending Legislature authorisation.

questions.q: Can money be spent on a new service from savings before a supplementary grant is obtained?
options: Yes, if there are savings within the grant
No, even if there are savings within the grant
Yes, if the Finance Department concurs
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 94(2): no expenditure on a new service before a supplementary grant.

questions.q: What token sum is shown if a new service can be met from savings in the grant?
options: Rs. 100, or the balance actually required
Rs. 10, or the balance actually required
Rs. 1,000, or the balance actually required
Rs. 500, or the balance actually required
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 94(2): a token sum (Rs. 100) or the balance required is shown.

questions.q: How is interim provision found for an urgent new service before a supplementary grant?
options: By a loan from the Public Account
By surrender of savings to the Finance Department
By an advance from the Contingency Fund
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 94(2): an advance from the Contingency Fund pending authorisation.

questions.q: Under which Article of the Constitution is the Contingency Fund created?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 96: created under Article 267 (2), like an imprest at the Governor's disposal.

questions.q: For urgent expenditure not on a new service with no savings, who may authorise it with Finance concurrence?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 95(3): the Administrative Department, with Finance Department concurrence.

lessons.title: Re-Appropriation (5)
lessons.source: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11 Definitions: Reappropriation; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 84(1); Kerala Budget Manual, Para 84(1) General restrictions; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 84(1)(ii); Kerala Budget Manual, Para 84(1)(iv); Kerala Budget Manual, Para 84(2); Kerala Budget Manual, Para 84, Note 1; Ke
points: Reappropriation is the transfer of funds from one unit of appropriation to another.
The power to reappropriate between minor heads within a grant is exclusively that of the Finance Department.
Administrative Departments of the Secretariat and Chief Controlling Officers listed in column 4 of Appendix 9 have this delegated power.
No. Reappropriation should not involve undertaking a recurring liability that extends beyond the current financial year.
No. Only Government in the Finance Department can sanction moving Plan funds to non-plan expenditure, or funds for Centrally Sponsored Plan Schemes.
No. Reappropriation is not allowed between grants, between charged and voted sections, or between revenue and capital sections of a grant.
The amount reappropriated should invariably be a multiple of Rs. 100.
An excess or saving under a unit not exceeding Rs. 100 need not be regularised, if the grant as a whole is not exceeded.
remember: Reappropriation is transfer of funds from one unit of appropriation to another.
Between minor heads within a grant: only Finance Department. Not allowed between grants.
Amount must be a multiple of Rs. 100; excess or saving up to Rs. 100 need not be regularised.

questions.q: What is reappropriation?
options: Sanction of a sum above the amount already authorised
Return of unspent funds to the Finance Department
Transfer of funds from one unit of appropriation to another
A grant to regularise past excess expenditure
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11: reappropriation is transfer from one unit of appropriation to another.

questions.q: Who alone can reappropriate between minor heads within a grant?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 84(1): exclusively the Finance Department.

questions.q: Can reappropriation involve a recurring liability extending beyond the current financial year?
options: Yes, if the Finance Department agrees
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 84(1)(ii): no recurring liability beyond the current year.

questions.q: Is reappropriation permissible between grants?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 84(2): none between grants, charged and voted, or revenue and capital sections.

questions.q: The amount reappropriated should invariably be a multiple of what?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 84, Note 1: a multiple of Rs. 100.

lessons.title: Re-Appropriation (6)
lessons.source: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 86(1) Form of application/sanction; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 93(1); Kerala Budget Manual, Para 93(1)(i); Kerala Budget Manual, Para 93(1)(ii)
points: The sanctioning authority draws up proceedings in Form KBM 22 and sends one copy direct to the Accountant General.
Reappropriation and resumption may be ordered only up to the financial year's last day, not after its expiry.
Proposals from Chief Controlling Officers and local bodies must reach the Administrative Department by 15th February.
Proposals must be received in the Finance Department from the Administrative Department by 25th February.
remember: Reappropriation sanction is in Form KBM 22; one copy goes direct to the Accountant General.
Reappropriation and resumption only up to the last day of the financial year, not after.
Proposals reach Administrative Department by 15th February and Finance Department by 25th February.

questions.q: Which form is used for proceedings sanctioning reappropriation?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 86(1): proceedings in Form KBM 22.

questions.q: To whom is one copy of the reappropriation proceedings sent direct?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 86(1): one copy direct to the Accountant General.

questions.q: By what date must proposals from Chief Controlling Officers reach the Administrative Department?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 93(1)(i): 15th February.

questions.q: By what date must proposals reach the Finance Department from the Administrative Department?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 93(1)(ii): 25th February.

questions.q: Up to when may reappropriation and resumption be ordered?
options: Up to two months after the year ends
Up to the last day of the financial year, not after its expiry
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 93(1): not after the expiry of the financial year.

lessons.title: Budget Estimates (7)
lessons.source: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11 Definitions: Revised estimate; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 15 Estimates should be on cash basis; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 2 Annual Financial Statement; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 20(3) Revised Estimate; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 20(5); Kerala Budget Manual, Para 3(2);
points: Article 202 requires a statement of estimated receipts and expenditure for each financial year to be laid before the Legislature.
Non-plan estimates are received by the 15th of September.
Plan and Revenue estimates are received by the 30th of November.
Administrative Departments forward comments on the estimates to Finance Department within ten days of receiving them.
Estimates are on a cash basis: only what is expected to be actually received or paid during the year, including arrears of past years.
A Revised Estimate is an estimate of probable revenue and expenditure of the current year, based on actuals so far and expected for the rest.
The Revised Estimate is prepared bearing in mind the actual expenditure during the first five months of the current year.
No. A Revised Estimate does not nullify the budget passed by the Legislature, nor authorise additional expenditure.
remember: Article 202: Annual Financial Statement laid before the Legislature.
Non-plan estimates by 15th September; Plan and Revenue estimates by 30th November.
Estimates are on cash basis. Revised Estimate uses first five months' actuals and does not authorise extra spending.

questions.q: Which Article requires the Annual Financial Statement to be laid before the Legislature?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 2: Article 202.

questions.q: By when are the Non-plan estimates received in the Finance Department?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 3(2): Non-plan estimates by 15th September.

questions.q: On what basis are budget estimates prepared?
options: Accrual basis, including liabilities not yet paid
Sanction basis, including all sanctions issued
Cash basis, what is expected to be actually received or paid, including arrears
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 15: cash basis, including arrears of past years.

questions.q: How many months of actual expenditure of the current year guide the Revised Estimate?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 20(3): first five months.

questions.q: Does a Revised Estimate authorise additional expenditure?
options: No, it does not nullify the budget nor authorise additional expenditure
Yes, up to the revised amount
Yes, with Finance Department sanction only
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 20(5).

lessons.title: Budget Estimates (8)
lessons.source: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 21 Budget estimate
points: The Revised Estimate for the current year forms the basis for preparing the Budget Estimate for the coming year, with allowance for special factors.
remember: The Revised Estimate for the current year is the basis for the next year's Budget Estimate.
Due allowance is made for any special factor.

questions.q: What forms the basis for preparing the Budget Estimate for the coming year?
options: The Budget Estimate of the previous year
The Revised Estimate for the current year
The Appropriation Accounts of the last year
The supplementary grants of the current year
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 21: the Revised Estimate is the basis.

questions.q: What is allowed for when the Revised Estimate is used as the basis for the next Budget Estimate?
options: Due allowance for any special factor
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 21: with due allowance for any special factor.

questions.q: Which estimate is used as the basis for the coming year's Budget Estimate?
options: Non-plan estimate of the coming year
Supplementary estimate of the previous year
Excess grant estimate of the previous year
Revised Estimate of the current year
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 21.

lessons.title: Registers
lessons.source: KAC Vol III, Art. 113 Register of Revenue; KAC Vol III, Art. 141 Register of Works; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 67 Appropriation Control; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 70(1) Disbursing Officers; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 70(2); Kerala Budget Manual, Para 71; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 72(6) Chief Contr
points: Each Disbursing Officer keeps a register of expenditure and liabilities in Form KBM 12.
A Disbursing Officer keeps a separate Liability Register in Form KBM 13.
A monthly statement in Form KBM 14 shows liabilities incurred, payments against them, liabilities cancelled and outstanding commitments.
A Subordinate Controlling Officer consolidates disbursement figures in Form KBM 15.
Every Controlling Officer must also maintain a Liability Register in Form KBM 13.
Treasury checks availability of budget provision in the Appropriation Control Register on each bill. If insufficient, the bill is returned uncashed.
Revenue receipts of the division are classified and abstracted in a Register of Revenue, K.P.W. Form 4, in the Divisional Office.
A permanent record of expenditure on all works in a year is kept in Registers of Works, K.P.W. Forms 38 and 39.
remember: Disbursing Officer: expenditure register KBM 12; Liability Register KBM 13; monthly statement to Controlling Officer KBM 14.
Subordinate Controlling Officer consolidates in KBM 15; Controlling Officers also keep KBM 13.
Treasury returns bill uncashed if appropriation is insufficient. PWD: Register of Revenue K.P.W. Form 4; Registers of Works Forms 38 and 39.

questions.q: In which form does a Disbursing Officer maintain the register of expenditure and liabilities?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 70(1): Form KBM 12.

questions.q: In which form is the separate Liability Register kept?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 70(2): Form KBM 13.

questions.q: Which form is the monthly statement of liabilities forwarded to the Controlling Officer?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 70(2): Form KBM 14.

questions.q: A Subordinate Controlling Officer consolidates disbursement figures in which form?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 71: Form KBM 15.

questions.q: What happens at the treasury if the available appropriation is insufficient to cover a bill?
options: The bill is cashed and reported to the Finance Department
The bill is kept pending until a supplementary grant
The bill is cashed from the Contingency Fund
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 67: the bill is returned uncashed.

lessons.title: Capital And Revenue
lessons.source: KAC Vol I, Art. 30-A(1) Allocation between Capital and Revenue; KAC Vol I, Art. 30-A(2); KAC Vol I, Art. 30-A(3); KAC Vol I, Art. 30-A(5); KAC Vol I, Art. 30-A(6); KAC Vol I, Art. 30-A(7); KAC Vol I, Art. 30-A(8)
points: Capital expenditure is spending meant to increase concrete assets of a material and permanent character, or to reduce or extinguish recurring liabilities.
The assets produced should belong to the authority incurring the expenditure. Grants-in-aid to local bodies for their own assets are not capital expenditure.
Expenditure on a temporary asset cannot ordinarily be considered as expenditure of a capital nature.
Capital bears all first construction and equipment charges, and intermediate maintenance charges while the work is not yet open for service.
Subject to the exceptions, revenue bears all later maintenance charges and all working expenses, meaning working and upkeep of the project.
For mixed renewal and replacement works, only the cost of genuine improvements may be debited to capital. Revenue provides for replacement of wastage.
Writing back of capitalised interest is the first charge on capital receipts or surplus revenue from the project once it is opened for working.
remember: Capital expenditure: increases concrete assets of a material and permanent character, or extinguishes or reduces recurring liabilities.
Assets must belong to the spending authority; grants-in-aid to local bodies are not capital; temporary assets are not capital.
Capital bears first construction and equipment; revenue bears later maintenance and working expenses.

questions.q: Capital expenditure is broadly expenditure to do what?
options: Meet the day-to-day working expenses of a project
Pay grants-in-aid to local bodies for their own assets
Increase concrete assets of a material and permanent character, or extinguish or reduce recurring liabilities
Create temporary assets of any value
questions.why: KAC Vol I, Art. 30-A(1).

questions.q: For spending to be capital, to whom must the assets produced belong?
questions.why: KAC Vol I, Art. 30-A(2): grants-in-aid for assets of local bodies are not capital.

questions.q: Can expenditure on a temporary asset ordinarily be considered capital?
options: Yes, if above a fixed amount
Yes, if the Finance Department agrees
questions.why: KAC Vol I, Art. 30-A(3).

questions.q: What should capital bear for a new project?
options: All later maintenance charges and working expenses
Only the cost of replacing wastage
First construction and equipment charges, and intermediate maintenance while not yet opened for service
questions.why: KAC Vol I, Art. 30-A(5).

questions.q: Subject to the exceptions, what should revenue bear after the project is opened?
options: All subsequent maintenance charges and working expenses
Only the cost of genuine improvements
questions.why: KAC Vol I, Art. 30-A(6).

lessons.title: Excess Grant
lessons.source: Kerala Budget Manual, Appendix 15, Procedure for regularisation of excesses; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11 Definitions: Excess grant; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 97(1) Excess grant; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 97(2)
points: An excess grant is a grant by the Legislative Assembly to regularise expenditure over the amount granted for a service in an earlier financial year.
Excess expenditure coming to notice after the financial year ends is always looked upon as an irregularity.
If expenditure is found after year end to exceed the grant as a whole, a demand for excess grant must be presented to the Legislature.
Administrative Departments submit notes explaining excesses to Audit within two months, after scrutiny by Finance Department.
Audit returns the notes, duly vetted, within a fortnight of receiving them.
Notes go to the Committee right after the Appropriation Accounts are presented to the Assembly, or on 10th April, whichever is later.
remember: Excess grant regularises expenditure above the amount granted in a previous financial year.
Excess expenditure noticed after year end is always an irregularity.
Notes on excesses: Administrative Departments to Audit within two months; Audit returns within a fortnight; to the Committee after Appropriation Accounts or 10th April, whichever is later.

questions.q: What is an excess grant?
options: A sum sanctioned over and above the amount already authorised in the current year
A transfer of funds from one unit of appropriation to another
Funds surrendered by a Disbursing Officer
A grant to regularise expenditure over the amounts granted for a service in a previous financial year
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11: excess grant regularises previous year's excess.

questions.q: How is excess expenditure noticed after the financial year ends looked upon?
options: As a matter for the Treasury alone
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 97(1).

questions.q: Within what time must Administrative Departments submit notes on excesses to Audit?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Appendix 15: within two months, after scrutiny by the Finance Department.

questions.q: Within what time does Audit return the vetted notes on excesses?
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Appendix 15: within a fortnight.

questions.q: When are the notes on excesses submitted to the Public Accounts Committee?
options: Before the Appropriation Accounts are presented
After the Appropriation Accounts are presented, or on 10th April, whichever is later
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Appendix 15.

lessons.title: Surrender And Resumption
lessons.source: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11 Definitions: Resumption; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11 Definitions: Surrender; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 91(1) Surrender of savings; Kerala Budget Manual, Para 92 Resumption of savings
points: Surrender is reporting back to Finance Department, through the Administrative Department, appropriation that is in excess of needs or left unspent.
All anticipated savings should be surrendered immediately when foreseen, without waiting for the year end, unless needed for definite excesses elsewhere.
Resumption is the Finance Department formally accepting funds found excess of requirements, from sums surrendered by the Controlling or Disbursing Officer.
First savings to the extent of any reduction made for probable savings are resumed, then the rest reappropriated, and finally the remainder resumed.
remember: Surrender: reporting back unspent or excess appropriation to the Finance Department through the Administrative Department.
Anticipated savings are surrendered immediately when foreseen, not at year end.
Resumption: Finance Department's formal acceptance of surrendered funds. Order: resume for probable-savings reduction, reappropriate, resume the rest.

questions.q: What is surrender of funds?
options: Reporting back to the Finance Department, through the Administrative Department, appropriation in excess of needs
Transfer of funds from one unit of appropriation to another
A grant to regularise earlier excess expenditure
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11: Surrender.

questions.q: When should anticipated savings be surrendered?
options: Only at the end of the financial year
Only after the Appropriation Accounts are prepared
Immediately they are foreseen, without waiting till the end of the year
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 91(1).

questions.q: What is resumption of funds?
options: Reporting back unspent funds to the Finance Department
Transfer of funds between minor heads
Formal acceptance by the Finance Department of funds found in excess, out of sums surrendered
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 11: Resumption.

questions.q: What does the Finance Department do first with reported savings where a reduction for probable savings was made?
options: Resumes savings to the extent needed to give effect to the reduction
Returns all savings to the Disbursing Officer
Surrenders them to the Accountant General
questions.why: Kerala Budget Manual, Para 92: first resumption, then reappropriation, then resumption of the remainder.
